desc:
A group of people must cross a river. weights[i] is the weight of person i. You have exactly boats boats available (using fewer is fine). Each boat carries at most two people and the total weight on a boat must not exceed a common weight limit L; a single person must weigh at most L as well.

Return the smallest integer L for which everyone can cross using at most boats boats. The input guarantees boats ≥ ceil(n / 2), so some limit always works.

weights = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], boats = 3
L = 5: boats (1,4), (2,3), (5)
result = 5

weights = [2, 9, 4, 7], boats = 3
result = 9
hints: For a fixed limit L, the minimum number of boats is the classic two-pointer greedy. The number of boats needed never increases as L grows. What does that suggest?
That gives binary search on L, but there is an even more direct way. With boats boats and n people, at least p = n - boats boats must carry two people.

Heavy people are best left to travel alone, so the paired people are the 2p lightest. Pair the lightest with the heaviest of those 2p, the second lightest with the second heaviest, and so on; the limit is the maximum of those pair sums and the heaviest person.
editorial: Every boat carries one or two people, so with boats boats at least p = n - boats boats must be shared (if p ≤ 0 everyone can travel alone and the answer is the heaviest weight). More shared boats than needed never help, since a shared boat can always be split into two single trips without raising the limit above the heaviest weight, which the limit must cover anyway.

Singles only force L ≥ their own weight, which is already implied by L ≥ max(weights). So it is best to make the lightest 2p people the shared ones: swapping a paired person for a lighter single can only lower the pair sum. Among those 2p sorted values, pairing smallest with largest, then the next smallest with the next largest, minimizes the largest pair sum (the standard exchange argument).

Hence L = max(w[n-1], max over i < p of w[i] + w[2p-1-i]). After sorting this is one two-pointer pass. An alternative with the same result is binary searching L and running the boat-counting greedy for each guess, in O(n log n log(sum)). The direct method is O(n log n) for the sort.
solution:
def minBoatLimit(weights, boats):
    w = sorted(weights)
    n = len(w)
    p = max(0, n - boats)
    limit = w[-1]
    i, j = 0, 2 * p - 1
    while i < j:
        s = w[i] + w[j]
        if s > limit:
            limit = s
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return limit
